Musk Calls Tesla's Merger Vote "Quite a High Hurdle." JPMorgan's Premium Math Puts the Stock Near $500. ©U.S. Air Force photo by Trevor Cokley and kb group via Canva

[IMAGE CREDIT: U.S. Air Force photo by Trevor Cokley and kb group via Canva]

Key Takeaways

Elon Musk said on SpaceX's Oct. 20 earnings call that a SpaceX-Tesla merger would need the votes of 50% of all Tesla shares, and that the two companies' special committees haven't agreed on terms.

JPMorgan expects a SpaceX-led all-stock deal at a typical 30% to 35% premium, which works out to about $486 to $505 a share on Tesla's $373.71 close.

If turnout matches the roughly 74% at Tesla's 2025 annual meeting, a deal would need about two-thirds of the votes cast.

Tesla's new auto-vote program for retail holders could narrow that gap, but it's brand new and no enrollment figures are public.

A lot of Tesla (TSLA:NASDAQ) investors treat a merger with SpaceX (SPCX:NASDAQ) as a done deal. Elon Musk isn't one of them.

Deutsche Bank's Edison Yu asked about a merger on SpaceX's earnings call Tuesday. Musk started with: "I feel like I'm tap dancing through a mine field."

Musk said both companies have set up special committees of independent directors, and he stays out of their talks as a conflicted party. He thinks a deal would be a good idea. Then he named the problem:

"particularly on the Tesla side, we will need a 50% vote of all shares, not just those who vote, but of all shareholders. And that's quite a high hurdle to try to achieve."

Wall Street has mostly skipped over that part.

JPMorgan expects a SpaceX-led all-stock deal at a typical 30% to 35% premium to Tesla's current valuation, a structure that would keep Musk in majority voting control of the combined company. On Tesla's $373.71 close Tuesday, that's about $486 to $505 a share.

See the full breakdown of Buy, Hold, and Sell ratings on Tesla, along with Wall Street's revenue and earnings estimates, all in one place. More than 500,000 investors use TIKR to research stocks like this one. See Tesla's Analyst Ratings

Every missing ballot counts as a no

Tesla needs a majority of all its shares, so any share that doesn't vote works against the deal.

And plenty of Tesla shares don't vote. Turnout at its 2025 annual meeting was about 74%, one of its best rates yet. At that turnout, a merger would need about 68% of the votes cast just to reach half of all shares.

Tesla has already seen how this plays out. In 2025, its proposal to drop its supermajority voting rules won about 54% of the shares that voted. That came to only 39.4% of all shares.

Barclays put broker non-votes at about 11% of Tesla's outstanding votes at that meeting. In its request to the SEC, Tesla cited Broadridge data showing that retail investors voted only 28% of their shares in the 2025 proxy season, against 76.6% for institutions. And few stocks have a retail following like Tesla's.

title: We Already Know Tesla Is Failing One Key Metric Before It Reports Earnings

[IMAGE CREDIT: U.S. Air Force photo by Trevor Cokley and Bl∡ke from Pexels via Canva]

Key Takeaways

Tesla deployed 13.7 GWh of energy storage in the third quarter, about 2.2 GWh short of the 15.9 GWh analysts expected, even as vehicle deliveries beat estimates.

Storage matters more than its share of revenue suggests, because Tesla's operating margin was just 1.4% in the second quarter.

Energy's gross margin had already fallen to 20.4% in the second quarter from 39.5% in the first, and Mike Snyder, who ran energy and charging, has reportedly left.

Tonight's call is the first chance to hear whether the shortfall is a matter of timing or the start of a slowdown.

Tesla (TSLA:NASDAQ) reports third-quarter results after the close today.

But one of the numbers that matters most is already out, and it came in light.

The miss behind the delivery beat

Tesla's Oct. 2 production report showed deliveries beating Wall Street's estimates. The energy storage figure in the same report got a lot less attention:

13.7 GWh deployed in the third quarter

About 15.9 GWh expected by analysts, so it came in 14% light

Up 9.6% from 12.5 GWh a year ago, and barely above the second quarter's 13.5 GWh

Still short of the 14.2 GWh record set in the fourth quarter of 2025

That flat quarter came even after a new factory in Texas started production in August.

See the full breakdown of Buy, Hold, and Sell ratings on Tesla, along with Wall Street's revenue and earnings estimates, all in one place. More than 500,000 investors use TIKR to research stocks like this one. See Tesla's Analyst Ratings

Storage has been carrying more than its share

Energy is the smaller business. It brought in $3.14 billion of Tesla's $28.24 billion in second-quarter revenue, about 11%. But it has mattered more as the margins on the rest of the company have shrunk.

Tesla (TSLA): gross margin (%), fiscal 2021–2025 (TIKR)

Gross margin dropped from 25.6% in 2022 to 18.0% in 2025, and it slipped again to 16.8% in the second quarter of 2026. The operating margin that quarter was 1.4%.

Energy's gross margin held up much better for a while: 39.5% in the first quarter. Then it fell to 20.4% in the second. Tesla pointed to warranty charges tied to a supplier's cell issue, one-time tariff benefits that didn't repeat, and lower prices for industrial storage as competition heats up.

So now both the volume and the pricing of storage are in question.

And then there's the leadership change. Mike Snyder, Tesla's vice president of energy and charging, has stepped down, [The Wall Street Journal reported](LINK NEEDED) on Oct. 15. Snyder joined Tesla in 2014 and rose to run the Megapack business. He took the top energy job in 2024, after longtime energy chief Drew Baglino left. AJ Booth, senior director of energy products engineering, is reportedly taking over, while Elon Musk steers Tesla toward AI and robotics.

Tesla just reported Q3 2026 with earnings per share of US$0.24 and net income of US$787m, and the stock barely flinched. Shares slipped about 0.6% over the last session, a muted move for a business that usually swings hard on any hint of good or bad news.

The real story sits in profitability. Trailing net margin has compressed to 3.1% while the valuation still prices in a rich revenue multiple. That gap between a premium P/S and thinner profits turns today's calm share price into a sentiment check on how much faith investors still place in Tesla's long runway.

title: What Investors Overlooked Before Intel's 127% Run
detail:
What Investors Overlooked Before Intel's 127% Run
Bailey Pemberton
Sat, October 24, 2026 at 10:10 AM EDT 4 min read
INTC
TSLA
GOOG
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Intel's year was defined by concrete deals, not just headlines, from Tesla's Terafab choosing its 14A process to Google's multi million TPU order that signaled real foundry demand. For Intel shareholders, the return over the past year was 127.2%, including dividends. If you were deciding whether to buy on 23 October 2025, what exactly did you need to believe about those early contracts and AI bets before the later earnings beats arrived?

Narratives are how investors here put a case on the record, with explicit assumptions about revenue, margins and the multiple. Those assumptions imply an estimated Fair Value.

Intel has already moved. Pinpoint other ways to investigate the theme among 55 AI infrastructure stocks.

The Argument Intel Investors Were Really Having

The shares cost US$38.16 at the start of the period. Anyone weighing Intel then was really choosing between two structured stories about where the chipmaker might be several years down the road.

The bullish Narrative put Fair Value at US$79, 107% above the start price. It rested on Intel's aggressive roadmap and a cyclical PC rebound, assuming revenue growth of 10.0% with profit margins reaching 22.0% over a 5 year stretch.

The more cautious Narrative set Fair Value at US$25.18, 34% below the start price. It treated Intel's reorganisation and AI focus as helpful but risky, assuming revenue growth of 3.5% and profit margins improving only to 7.8% over 3 years.

NasdaqGS:INTC 1-Year Stock Price Chart
What The Evidence Did To The Intel Argument

Intel's biggest new fact was contract and product traction. Google's multi million TPU order, Terafab's choice of 14A and rising AI CPU demand supported the bullish case that real customers would show up. The reported numbers were less clean. Revenue reached US$16.13b in Q2 2026 versus US$12.86b in Q2 2025, yet the firm still reported a larger loss and a net margin that moved deeper into negative territory.

The lesson for other stocks is simple. When a thesis leans on a profitability fix, treat contract wins and upbeat AI stories as separate from the core test. Check whether net margin, not just sales, is trending toward the level the original Narrative needed.

What Intel's Price Already Bakes In

Intel trades at US$86.96 today, far above where the earlier debate began, while the selected cautious Narrative now puts its Fair Value below that market level. The Narrative credits the turnaround plan and breadth in AI chips but questions how much of that promise can realistically be captured.

A buyer here is effectively assuming Intel converts its roadmap and contracts into durable AI and CPU economics. The open question is how that belief holds up against the Narrative's emphasis on manufacturing execution risk and intense competition in x86 and accelerators.

title: Rivian Shines as a Bright Spot in a Down U.S. EV Market, and Surprisingly, It's Not All R2 Driven
detail:
Rivian Shines as a Bright Spot in a Down U.S. EV Market, and Surprisingly, It's Not All R2 Driven
Daniel Miller, The Motley Fool

RIVN
TSLA
NVDA

Trading disclosure

Registration data can be a helpful tool for investors trying to glean more information from automakers' sales trends. It probably isn't explained enough, but vehicle registration data serves as a proxy for vehicle sales. It provides a more inclusive and detailed look at model information, as some automakers don't break out U.S. sales from global numbers, and/or don't report monthly. The catch is that it can lag other sales data by about a month.

With that said, let's take a look at the newest data that highlights Rivian Automotive's (NASDAQ: RIVN) surge toward the top during a rough overall month, trailing only Tesla (NASDAQ: TSLA) in August EV registrations.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Image source: Rivian.
Show me the data!

There are a lot of key takeaways for investors in the EV registration data, which, for the record, doesn't include hybrids, only full battery electric vehicles (EVs). Scratching the surface of August data, it initially appears to have been a brutal month for EV sales in the U.S., recording a sharp 36% decline compared to the prior year. But remember that is right when car buyers were jumping all over EV purchases before a Sept. 30, 2025, expiration of the $7,500 federal EV tax credit.

Going forward, after one more month of skewed year-over-year comparisons, the picture should be much clearer regarding the U.S. EV industry's health.

Rivian, along with Toyota, was a clear bright spot in late-summer registrations. Thanks in part to Rivian launching its highly anticipated R2 in June, the company jumped from No. 10 in U.S. EV registrations a year ago up to No. 2, trailing only Tesla. The good news for Rivian investors is that August was still in the early innings of accelerating production of the R2, and the company added a second production shift late in the third quarter, which won't show up in registration data in full until October's data is collected and released. That means Rivian may not give up its No. 2 spot for some time, especially considering that a third production shift is planned next year.

The good news for Rivian is not all R2-driven

Don't get me wrong; Rivian's data was certainly boosted by the addition of R2 registration data, where none existed in the prior year, but it wasn't the only reason for Rivian's surge higher. Rivian's R2 recorded 1,554 registrations in August, a figure that will again be boosted by increased efficiency, additional shifts, and the upcoming launch of lower-priced R2 trims. Remember, Rivian's R2 launch process began by producing and delivering its most expensive, and likely more profitable, models/trims first.

Tesla Inc. is directing recent tariff refunds toward expanding its United States manufacturing capacity, according to Chief Financial Officer Vaibhav Taneja. Chief Executive Officer Elon Musk and Taneja detailed this strategy during the company's third-quarter earnings call, emphasizing the physical labor required to scale domestic operations.

Channeling Tariff Refunds

Tesla reported that energy gross margins improved sequentially from 20.4% to 33.1% in the third quarter. Taneja stated this increase is "primarily attributed to tariff refunds recognized in the quarter and warranty true-downs resulting from alignment with our vendor on certain cell-related costs to be reimbursed by them."

The company plans to use this capital to increase its domestic manufacturing footprint. "The money that we received from the tariff refunds is being reinvested to expand production capacity in the U.S.," Taneja said.

Taneja set expectations for the physical execution of this expansion, stating, "I'd like to stress that we like to do a lot of hardcore, real grunt work to get production facilities up and running."

Looking ahead, Taneja noted that capital expenditures "for the next few years would continue to expand as we add more Robotaxi fleet, we expand our production capacity for Optimus, install manufacturing capacity for solar, purchase additional AI compute infrastructure, and build a semiconductor fab."

Expanding Factory Footprint

Musk outlined long-term vehicle production targets, stating Tesla is "aiming for 5 million vehicles a year by approximately 2030." Musk said the company is "laying the groundwork for a lot more manufacturing capacity" to achieve this volume.

Part of this infrastructure includes the Austin-based Terafab project. Musk stated that the research fab is "progressing quickly" and that Tesla will "begin commissioning machinery in the first half of next year."

Analyst Ray Wang, who is the founder of Silicon Valley-based Constellation Research, said on Wednesday that a merger between Space Exploration Technologies Corp. and Tesla Inc. would help Elon Musk develop technologies he is aiming for.

Anything Elon Musk Touches Grows '10x,' Ray Wang Says

During an interview with CNBC, Wang said that there were a "lot of synergies" in what SpaceX and Tesla are working towards, be it self-driving or battery technology or more. When asked about a merger, Wang said that he did see such a deal going through.

Wang pointed to SpaceX's dual-class share structure as the reason why Musk wanted to use the company as the vehicle for the merger. Notably, Musk holds over 80% of SpaceX's voting rights.

Following a merger, Musk would see "37% of equity and 56% of the voting rights in a combined entity," Wang said, adding that "Tesla shareholders might get 0.7 SpaceX shares for each Tesla share," which gives Musk a chance to take back the companies and reach the "engineering synergies that he's hoping to reach."

When asked if a merger would be supported by big SpaceX investors like the Saudi Arabian Sovereign Wealth Fund PIF, Wang said that they should. "Almost everything that Elon Musk touches gives you 10x scale, 100x scale, 1000x scale," he said.

He also said that challenges include future compute contracts for SpaceX and Tesla, as well as getting the "engineers together and then getting everyone together to have one common roadmap."

Wang then said he sees SpaceX's price target to be $300 as demand for its compute increases.

This could imply around 90% upside for SpaceX's stock, based on its current share price of about $155 during pre-market trading on Thursday.

Wang noted that "long-term upside is in…telecommunications" for SpaceX.

The Democrats are hoping to regain congressional power in November's midterm elections, and doing so means they could potentially launch investigations into the world's richest man.

From his role in the Trump administration to the growing influence of SpaceX [NASDAQ: SPCX] and Tesla [NASDAQ: TSLA], Democrats have long been eyeing Elon Musk and his vast business network and, according to Politico, the list of possible investigations into Musk is growing.

The billionaire appears to be getting ahead of the potential probes, vowing retribution against any Democrat who takes action against him.

"Live by the sword, die by the sword," Musk wrote on X, replying to a post featuring Politico's article. "Those who pick fights with me should understand that I will find out who is really pulling the strings and come for them, not just their puppets."

According to Politico, Democrats are weighing investigations into Musk's time leading the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) and his government contracts, as well as his alleged role in placing restrictions on SpaceX's Starshield networks in Ukraine, which are used by the Ukrainian military.

Musk's role in DOGE

DOGE was established within days of Trump's inauguration, and Musk was tasked with heading the department that was meant to reign in alleged government overspending.

Politico is reporting that members of House Oversight and other panels are looking to examine Musk's role in the department, which saw the removal of over 250,000 federal jobs and the dismantling of USAID.

The billionaire originally claimed DOGE would reduce government spending by $2 trillion, but later scaled it back to $1 trillion before saying it would save roughly $150 billion in the 2025 financial year. DOGE's official government website claims it saved $215 billion, though critics have said the number is exaggerated.

Musk admitted in an Oct. 20 interview with "The Builders" podcast that he got "carried away" while working with the Trump administration, agreeing with the host that he appeared to get "too intoxicated" by his proximity to power.

"Yeah, I think that's true," said Musk. "I got carried away, basically."
